newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK FARMERS OCCUPY SMALLER ROADS, HIGHWAYS FREE.
newsitem.headline: GREEK FARMERS OCCUPY SMALLER ROADS, HIGHWAYS FREE.

text.p: Greek farmers occupied with some 2,000 tractors small roads in central Greece on Tuesday but main highways were kept open by riot police units.

Convoys of hundreds of tractors were turned back by police in this central Thessally region after farmers managed to drive some of them on the main north-south highway and briefly occupy it in two positions.
There were no clashes, eyewitnesses said.
"We continue our struggle. The first day went well despite the strong police presence which aimed to terrorise the farmers," farmers' representative Thanasis Nasikas told reporters.

The farmers' main block, with more than 1,500 tractors, was outside Drougos village south of Larissa where they occupied an old north-south road. Police said no cars were stranded and that the effect on traffic was minimal.
"Truckers and most motorists don't drive on the old national road. As long as highways are kept open we don't have any problems," a police official said.

Several convoys of hundreds of tractors played a game of hide-and-seek with police throughout the day, drawing them into farm fields and getting them stuck away from their guarding points in an effort to reach the highways.
The government successfully waited out a crippling 25-day farmers' road blockade in December, which virtually cut the country in two, but has now vowed to keep roads free.
"We have every legal right to take measures to preserve normalcy. We want to prevent a road blockade," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.
The government threatened to use force if necessay to thwart a new attempt to block with roads. The farmers vowed to continue with their plans but announced they would not clash with police.
About 5,000 police, many in riot gear, and helicopters were dispatched to the area to prevent the farmers from taking over the roads for a second time.
"Terrorism does not work on farmers. Their problems are so deep that all the helicopters and police will not hinder them," Vangelis Boutas, another farmers' representative, told reporters.

The farmers had given up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel and tax cuts were not met.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis has turned down most of their demands, saying the state budget could not affort to spend an extra drachma on any specific group.
He said his strict 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, tight new incomes and tax policies, were necessary to turn the ailing economy around.
